name: Best Hardware (2026 name)
also_known_as: Best Hardware Project / Best Hardware Special Award (the 2016 to 2019 results pages use both forms)
file_note: A precedents file, not a winners file. These four projects were chosen for how well they document an instrument like ours, not for having won a prize, and none of them won Best Hardware. `verified` means the pages were rendered from the live URLs and read in full, and that every award or section claim in `note` was checked against the iGEM results page cited there. Where a track could not be read off a results page it is null rather than guessed. The Best Hardware winners of 2023 to 2025 are covered separately in research/hardware.* by a sibling agent; these four sit deliberately outside that set.
ballot: Does the hardware you developed address a need or problem in synthetic biology?
Did the team conduct user testing and learn from user feedback?
Did the team demonstrate utility and functionality in their hardware proof of concept?
Is the documentation of the hardware system sufficient to enable reproduction by other teams?

winners.note: Photometer precedent 1, project 'Cellock Holmes'. The OD/F Device: a 3D-printed cuvette holder in a laser-cut acrylic case, a 600 nm LED and a TSL235R-LF light-to-frequency sensor, reading OD600 and GFP fluorescence in one body for a stated $60. Chosen because it is the most completely reproducible photometer write-up in iGEM. It carries a quantity by component by unit-cost by line-total table in euros and dollars with a dated exchange rate and live vendor links, downloadable STL, laser-cut SVG and two Arduino sketches, a twelve-step photographic construction manual, a two-stage calibration onto a lab photospectrometer with its regression coefficients given and averaged, and a prior-art paragraph naming what earlier DIY turbidity meters failed to document. It is also the ancestor of the lineage this bank follows: Aachen's own 2015 in-line biomass sensor cites it, Tsinghua-A 2018 credits it by name, and TU Darmstadt 2019 lists it among the OD600 sensors it set out to improve on. Track not confirmed: the 2014 results page returns 59 words when rendered, so no section is claimed; the team's own Achievements page confirms it competed in the Measurement Track. Three pages rendered: the project page, Notebook/Engineering/ODF (technical detail, costed BOM, construction manual) and Interlab_Study/Hardware (parts list and the sensor-linearity argument).

Photometer precedent 2. The SensorBrick: an in-line OD600 sensor built from a drilled polystyrene cuboid with plastic optical fibre carrying light from an LED across the bore to a six-wavelength spectral sensor, plumbed between the bioreactor and a syringe pump so the sample sits still while it is read. The closest architectural match to our photometer in the bank, and the best limitation writing found anywhere in the search: it calibrates against a bench photometer, reports the correlation, then runs two further experiments to check the transform, finds that its own sensor reads low, diagnoses why (it was calibrated on a strain expressing sfGFP, whose fluorescence added light at 600 nm), and concludes that the sensor cannot be calibrated once for all strains and that its output should be treated as qualitative. CAD files and firmware are on GitLab, and the page names the two outside open-source projects it built on. Track confirmed OG: the 2019 results page places TU Darmstadt in the Overgrad section in four separate award and nominee listings (https://2019.igem.org/Results). Not a Best Hardware winner or nominee.

Bioreactor precedent 1. A DIY chemostat: a 10 mL working-volume reactor with 3D-printed peristaltic pumps characterised over 0.5 to 1400 mL/h, a magnet-and-DC-motor stirrer calibrated over 200 to 1400 rpm, and an in-line continuous OD unit reading 605 nm through a glass flow path so nothing is withdrawn to measure. Chosen for the one thing no other candidate had: a characterisation page that reports a real continuous-culture run with dilution-rate step changes (batch to OD 1.0, then D = 0.1, 0.3 and 0.4 per hour held for three reactor volumes each), and reports a control fault found mid-run with the fix and its measured cost in OD. Its construction manuals index carries a subsystem-by-subsystem cost table to a 384.81 EUR total for three complete reactors, with a dated exchange rate and numbered vendor references, and the laser-cut, rotor-STL and firmware archives still download (five checked, all valid, 809 bytes to 475 KB). CC-BY-SA on every page. Track not confirmed: the 2015 results page returns 365 words when rendered. Five pages rendered: the hardware page, Characterization_of_Bioreactor, the Construction_Manuals index, and the Biomass_Sensor and Pumps manuals.

Bioreactor precedent 2. The openPBR: an open-source flat-panel photobioreactor and turbidostat for Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, in nine-vessel or three-panel configurations, 15 to 30 mm path and 95 to 190 mL, with an OPT101 sensor rail reading online optical density against 680 nm LEDs from 400 to 800 nm. Chosen for the two things our own pages are weakest on. It gives a costed bill of materials broken down by subsystem to a 588 EUR total with a stated reason for publishing it, and it points at a GitHub project that holds assembly instructions, parts list and software together under a tagged release. Its OD section is also the only one in the bank that does the full chain in order: a calibration recipe written as instructions, then a validation on fresh samples plotted against an identity line, then the range over which the instrument stops being trustworthy. Track confirmed OG: the 2019 results page lists Humboldt Berlin as the Overgrad winner of Best Plant Synthetic Biology (https://2019.igem.org/Results). Not a Best Hardware winner or nominee.
